title: Failure to Comply Penalty Calculator | Subsection 162(7)
content:
Penalties

Failure to Comply Penalty Calculator

The one penalty in the set whose base is nothing at all, which is why it is the one a corporation owing $0.00 still has to watch.

Greater of $100.00 and $25.00 a dayCounted to 100 daysNot a percentage of taxSubsection 162(7)

Written and reviewed by Sharad Gondaliya, CPA (Ontario), CPA Ontario Membership 61040184.

Start Nil T2 Filing NOW

Last reviewed: November 23, 2026

The failure

Enter the days and answer the question above.

Gondaliya CPA Professional Corporation is a registered EFILE electronic filer. Returns are prepared and transmitted in Canada. Credentials are never shared and never used offshore.

The Greater of $100.00 and $25.00 a Day, Counted to 100 Days

Subsection 162(7) is the residual penalty in the Income Tax Act. It reaches a failure to file an information return when no other provision covers it, and a failure to comply with any other duty or obligation the Act or the Regulations impose. The charge is the greater of $100.00 and $25.00 multiplied by the number of days the failure continues, with the day count stopping at 100.

Two things follow from that shape. The first four days all cost $100.00, because four days at $25.00 is exactly the floor and anything shorter is below it. And the charge stops growing at $2,500.00, which it reaches on the hundredth day, however many years the failure then continues.

The failure continues$25.00 a dayPenalty under 162(7)
1 day$25.00$100.00
3 days$75.00$100.00
4 days$100.00$100.00
5 days$125.00$125.00
20 days$500.00$500.00
100 days$2,500.00$2,500.00
365 daysCounted to 100 days$2,500.00

Five Penalties, and the Base Each One Multiplies

Most of the late-filing provisions people have in mind are percentages of an amount of tax. This one is not, and that single difference is why it matters to a corporation with nothing to report.

ProvisionWhat it chargesWhat it multiplies
162(1), a late return of income5% of the unpaid tax, plus 1% a month to 12 monthsTax unpaid at the due date
162(2), a repeated failure after a demand10% of the unpaid tax, plus 2% a month to 20 monthsTax unpaid at the due date
162(7), a failure to complyThe greater of $100.00 and $25.00 a day to 100 daysNothing. It is a flat and daily amount
162(7.01), an information return with slipsA daily rate set by the slip count, with a floor and a ceilingNothing. The slip count picks the band
163(2), gross negligence50% of the understated tax, subject to a minimumTax that was understated

The two percentage provisions are run by the T2 late filing penalty calculator and the repeated failure to file penalty calculator. The slip scale is run by the T4 late filing penalty calculator, and subsection 163(2) has a checker of its own in the list below. The guide to T2 late filing penalties sets out how they interact.

Why This Is the Provision a Dormant Corporation Watches

A true nil return carries no percentage late-filing penalty, because that penalty is a percentage of tax owing and the corporation owes $0.00. That is a real and useful point, and it is also the point people stop at. The exposure on a quiet corporation is not the percentage provisions at all. It is the flat ones, the ones that do not ask what is owed.

The unfiled year also stays open indefinitely, invites a demand to file and then an arbitrary assessment, and blocks the clearance certificate a dissolution needs. The CRA demand to file deadline calculator and the arbitrary assessment response checker cover that sequence, and a non-resident-owned corporation has its own daily charge, which the non-resident T2 penalty calculator computes.

Nil T2 filing at $300.00 plus applicable sales tax per tax year covers the federal corporate income tax return for one tax year, and each unfiled year is its own return at that fee. Where a charge has already been assessed, the taxpayer relief eligibility checker sets out the grounds for having it reconsidered, and a voluntary disclosure is the other route where the filings themselves are the problem.

A percentage of nothing is nothing, which is exactly why the flat and daily charges are the ones a dormant corporation has to watch.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much is the penalty under subsection 162(7)?

The greater of $100.00 and $25.00 multiplied by the number of days the failure continues, with the day count stopping at 100. That puts it between $100.00 and $2,500.00.

Does it depend on how much tax is owing?

No. It is a flat and daily amount, which is what makes it the provision that still reaches a corporation owing $0.00.

What is the maximum?

$2,500.00. The day count stops at 100, so the figure does not grow after the hundredth day.

Is there a minimum?

Yes, $100.00. The first four days all come to $100.00, because four days at $25.00 is the floor exactly.

Does it apply to a late T2 return?

A return of income is charged under subsection 162(1) instead. This provision is the residual one, for information returns no other provision covers and for other duties under the Act.

Does it apply to late T4 slips?

No. An information return carrying slips is charged on the sliding scale in subsection 162(7.01), which is set by the slip count.

What kind of failure does it actually cover?

A failure to file an information return that no other provision reaches, and a failure to comply with another duty or obligation the Act or the Regulations impose.

Can it be charged on a nil year?

It can. Nothing in the provision asks whether any tax was payable, which is the difference between it and the percentage provisions.

Can it be cancelled?

Relief can be requested on the statutory grounds, and the request reaches back ten years. Cancelling a charge is discretionary rather than automatic, so the request has to be made on one of those grounds.

Does the nil T2 fee cover an assessed penalty?

No. The fee covers preparing and transmitting the corporate income tax return. An amount the Agency has already assessed sits outside it.

title: Schedule 1 Net Income Reconciliation Calculator
content:
Schedules

Schedule 1 Net Income Reconciliation Calculator

The one arithmetic step between the accounting profit and the figure the corporate return actually taxes, item by item.

Line 9999 to line 300Amortisation added backCapital cost allowance deductedHalf of meals added back

Written and reviewed by Sharad Gondaliya, CPA (Ontario), CPA Ontario Membership 61040184.

Start Nil T2 Filing NOW

Last reviewed: November 23, 2026

The reconciliation

Enter the accounting figure and leave the rest at zero on a nil year.

Gondaliya CPA Professional Corporation is a registered EFILE electronic filer. Returns are prepared and transmitted in Canada. Credentials are never shared and never used offshore.

What Schedule 1 Sits Between

The financial statements and the tax return disagree, on purpose. The statements are prepared to an accounting standard and the return is prepared to the Income Tax Act, and the two treat several ordinary items differently. Schedule 1 is where that disagreement is written down and resolved.

It starts at the net income or loss on line 9999 of Schedule 125, adds back what the statements deducted and the Act does not allow, deducts what the Act allows and the statements did not, and ends at net income for income tax purposes on line 300 of the T2. Everything the return then computes runs from line 300, not from the accounting figure.

ItemIn the statementsOn the returnSchedule 1
Amortisation and depreciationDeductedNot deductibleAdded back
Capital cost allowanceNot shownDeductible on Schedule 8Deducted
Meals and entertainmentDeducted in fullHalf of it allowedHalf added back
Club dues and membership feesDeductedNot deductibleAdded back
Fines and penaltiesDeductedGenerally not deductibleAdded back
Non-deductible reservesDeductedNot deductible unless the Act allows itAdded back

The Two Items That Account for Most of It

Amortisation is the largest reconciling item on most returns and the easiest to describe. The statements write an asset down on whatever basis the accountant considers reasonable. The Act ignores that figure entirely and substitutes capital cost allowance, computed by class at a prescribed rate on Schedule 8. So the accounting figure comes out and the tax figure goes in, and the two are rarely the same.

Meals and entertainment is the one most often missed. The statements carry the whole cost as an expense; the Act allows half of it. The other half is added back on Schedule 1 every year, which on a modest expense account is a small number that nonetheless has to be there.

Where no asset is owned there is no amortisation and no capital cost allowance, and the Schedule 8 CCA requirement checker settles whether the schedule is needed at all. The Schedule 125 checker and the Schedule 141 checker cover the two statements this one reconciles, and the guide to the GIFI schedules covers the set.

Schedule 1 is a bridge rather than a second income statement: it starts at the accounting figure and ends at the one the return taxes.

A Nil Year Has Nothing to Reconcile

On a year with no revenue and no expenses the accounting figure is $0.00, there is no amortisation to add back and no capital cost allowance to deduct, and line 300 is $0.00 as well. The reconciliation has nothing to do, which is the honest description of the schedule on a dormant corporation rather than a reason to leave it out of the thinking.

A year with expenses and no revenue is different, and it is the one worth being careful about. The statements show a loss, the loss may or may not be deductible, and line 300 is then a negative figure that carries forward. The expenses only year checker covers whether such a year is nil at all, and the required schedules checker lists what the return then carries.

Nil T2 filing at $300.00 plus applicable sales tax per tax year includes the GIFI schedules where they are required, Schedule 50 and Schedule 24 on a first return. The guide to T2 schedules on a nil return sets out the whole set, and the nil GIFI balance sheet checker covers the balance sheet side.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Schedule 1 for?

It reconciles the net income on the financial statements to net income for income tax purposes, which is line 300 of the T2.

Where does the starting figure come from?

Line 9999 of Schedule 125, the income statement information.

Why is amortisation added back?

Because the Act does not allow it. Capital cost allowance, computed by class on Schedule 8, is deducted in its place.

How much of meals and entertainment is added back?

Half. The statements carry the full cost and the Act allows fifty per cent of it.

Are club dues deductible?

No, so they are added back on Schedule 1 along with the other amounts the Act disallows.

What does Schedule 1 look like on a nil year?

It carries $0.00 through. There is no accounting income and nothing to reconcile, so line 300 is $0.00.

Can line 300 be negative?

Yes. A year with expenses and no revenue produces a loss for tax purposes, which carries forward rather than disappearing.

Is Schedule 1 the same as Schedule 125?

No. Schedule 125 is the income statement itself. Schedule 1 is the reconciliation that starts where Schedule 125 ends.

Does the nil T2 fee include it?

Yes, along with the GIFI schedules where they are required, Schedule 50 and Schedule 24 on a first return.

What if the accounting and tax figures are the same?

Then the schedule carries the figure through unchanged, which is the ordinary case on a corporation with nothing to reconcile.

title: GST/HST Filing Frequency Calculator | Reporting Periods
content:
GST/HST

GST/HST Filing Frequency Calculator

Two thresholds decide whether a registrant files annually, quarterly or monthly, and the deadline moves with the answer.

$1,500,000 and $6,000,000Annual, quarterly or monthlyOne month or threeElections shorten only

Written and reviewed by Sharad Gondaliya, CPA (Ontario), CPA Ontario Membership 61040184.

Start Nil T2 Filing NOW

Last reviewed: November 23, 2026

The registrant

Enter the taxable supplies and answer the question above.

Gondaliya CPA Professional Corporation is a registered EFILE electronic filer. Returns are prepared and transmitted in Canada. Credentials are never shared and never used offshore.

Two Figures Decide It, and Nothing Else Does

A registrant does not choose a reporting period from a standing start. The period is assigned by annual taxable supplies, and there are only two numbers in the test. At $1,500,000 or less the assigned period is annual. Above that and up to $6,000,000 it is quarterly. Above $6,000,000 it is monthly.

From the assigned period a registrant may elect a shorter one, never a longer one. An annual filer can elect quarterly or monthly, a quarterly filer can elect monthly, and a monthly filer has nothing shorter to move to. The supplies figure is worldwide and includes the supplies of associated persons, which is the part that catches a group of small corporations under common control.

Annual taxable suppliesAssigned periodMay electReturn due
$1,500,000 or lessAnnualMonthly or quarterlyThree months after the fiscal year end
More than $1,500,000 up to $6,000,000QuarterlyMonthlyOne month after the quarter ends
More than $6,000,000MonthlyNone availableOne month after the month ends

The Annual Filer Gets Three Months, the Others One

The deadline is not a fixed number of days from the period end. A monthly or quarterly filer has one month after the period closes to file and to pay. An annual filer has three months after the fiscal year end for both. That is a real difference and it is the reason the period matters to a quiet corporation at all.

There is one condition attached to annual filing. Where net tax for the year reaches $3,000.00, the annual filer also pays quarterly instalments through the year and the return reconciles them at the end. A registrant with nothing to remit never reaches that figure, so a dormant corporation on annual filing has one nil return a year and nothing in between.

The supplies set the frequency, an election can only make the periods shorter, and a dormant registrant still files on whichever one applies.

A Nil Return Is Still a Return, Once Per Period

Nothing about being dormant changes the assigned frequency. A monthly filer that stopped trading still has twelve returns a year to file, each of them at nil, until either the frequency is changed or the account is closed. That is the single strongest argument for electing or reverting to annual filing before a corporation goes quiet.

The GST/HST nil filing checker settles whether the return is owed, the GST/HST nil return deadline calculator dates it once the period is known, and the GST/HST account closure checker covers closing the account so the periods stop arriving. Where the question is whether an account has to exist at all, the GST/HST registration requirement checker runs the $30,000.00 small supplier test.

This is the sales tax account, which is not the corporate income tax return. Nil T2 filing at $300.00 plus applicable sales tax per tax year covers the T2 for one tax year and no GST/HST filing is part of it. The guide to CRA accounts on a dormant corporation covers every account a quiet corporation still carries, and the CRA account closure sequencer sets out the order they come off in.

Frequently Asked Questions

How is the GST/HST reporting period decided?

By annual taxable supplies. At $1,500,000 or less the assigned period is annual, above that to $6,000,000 it is quarterly, and above $6,000,000 it is monthly.

Can a registrant choose a different period?

A shorter one, yes. An annual filer may elect quarterly or monthly and a quarterly filer may elect monthly. A longer period than the assigned one is not available.

When is a quarterly return due?

One month after the quarter ends, for both the return and the payment.

When is an annual return due?

Three months after the fiscal year end for a corporation, for both the return and the payment.

Do associated corporations count in the supplies figure?

Yes. The test is worldwide taxable supplies including those of associated persons, which is what catches a group of small corporations.

Does a dormant registrant still file?

Yes, once per period in the assigned frequency, at nil, until the frequency changes or the account is closed.

What are the instalments an annual filer pays?

Where net tax for the year reaches $3,000.00 the annual filer pays quarterly instalments and the return reconciles them. A registrant with nothing to remit does not reach that figure.

Is a monthly filer that stopped trading stuck with twelve returns?

Until the frequency is changed or the account is closed, yes. That is the usual reason to deal with the frequency before a corporation goes quiet.

Is the GST/HST return part of the nil T2 fee?

No. The fee covers the federal corporate income tax return. The sales tax account is a separate filing to a separate programme.

Does the fiscal year end matter?

For an annual filer it sets the deadline, because the three months run from it. For monthly and quarterly filers the period end does.

title: Payroll Remittance Due Date Calculator | Remitter Types
content:
Payroll

Payroll Remittance Due Date Calculator

Four remitter types, two thresholds between them, and a withholding figure from two calendar years ago that decides which one applies.

Four remitter types$25,000 and $100,000Two calendar years backWeekend and holiday shift

Written and reviewed by Sharad Gondaliya, CPA (Ontario), CPA Ontario Membership 61040184.

Start Nil T2 Filing NOW

Last reviewed: November 23, 2026

The payroll

Enter the withholding figure and the pay date.

Gondaliya CPA Professional Corporation is a registered EFILE electronic filer. Returns are prepared and transmitted in Canada. Credentials are never shared and never used offshore.

Four Remitter Types, and Two Thresholds Between Them

There is no single payroll remittance deadline. There are four schedules, and which one a corporation is on depends on its average monthly withholding amount: the total of its remittances for a calendar year divided by the number of months it remitted. Two thresholds split the four, at $25,000.00 and at $100,000.00.

The regular remitter has the deadline most people know, the 15th of the month after the month of payment. Above $25,000.00 the schedule becomes twice monthly and above $100,000.00 four times monthly, and at that point the dates stop being calendar dates and become working-day counts.

Remitter typeAverage monthly withholding amountHow oftenDue
QuarterlyUnder $3,000.00 with a perfect compliance recordOnce a quarterThe 15th of the month after the quarter ends
RegularUnder $25,000.00Once a monthThe 15th of the month after the month of payment
Accelerated, threshold 1$25,000.00 to $99,999.99Twice a monthThe 25th for the 1st to the 15th, the 10th of the next month for the 16th to the end
Accelerated, threshold 2$100,000.00 or moreFour times a monthThe third working day after the 7th, the 14th, the 21st and the last day of the month

The Figure That Sets the Type Is Two Years Old

This is the part that catches people, and it catches them in exactly one direction. The average monthly withholding amount used for the current year is the one from two calendar years ago. A corporation that has wound its payroll down to nothing can therefore still be an accelerated remitter, on a twice-monthly or four-times-monthly schedule, because the test looks at a year when the payroll was running.

It cuts the other way too. A payroll that has grown sharply is not moved onto a faster schedule until the two-year lag catches up. Neither direction is something the employer chooses; the Agency sets the type and notifies it, and the quarterly schedule in the first row is assigned rather than elected.

Where a due date falls on a Saturday, a Sunday or a public holiday, the remittance is on time if it reaches the Agency on the next business day. The CRA account standing checker covers what the Agency currently shows for each account, and the guide to CRA accounts on a dormant corporation covers the set of them.

The remitter type is set by what the payroll looked like two years ago rather than what it looks like now, which is how a wound-down payroll ends up on an accelerated schedule.

When Nothing Was Paid, There Is Still a Period to Report

An open payroll account does not go quiet because the payroll did. The account keeps its periods, and where no remuneration was paid in a period the sensible course is to report that period at nil rather than to send nothing, because sending nothing is what produces a non-filing notice and an estimate. The payroll nil remittance checker covers that, and the T4 nil filing requirement checker covers whether the annual slip return is owed as well.

Where the payroll has stopped for good, closing the account is what ends the periods. The payroll account closure checker sets out what has to be done first and the CRA account closure sequencer sets out the order the accounts come off in, which matters because closing them in the wrong order leaves filings owed on an account that no longer accepts them.

Payroll is a separate programme account from corporate income tax. Nil T2 filing at $300.00 plus applicable sales tax per tax year covers the federal corporate income tax return for one tax year, and no payroll remittance or slip return is part of that fee. Where a slip return has gone in late, the T4 late filing penalty calculator computes the charge.

Frequently Asked Questions

When is a payroll remittance due?

For a regular remitter, the 15th of the month after the month the employees were paid. The accelerated schedules are more frequent than that.

What is the average monthly withholding amount?

The total of the remittances for a calendar year divided by the number of months the corporation remitted in it.

Which year does that figure come from?

Two calendar years before the current one, which is why a shrinking payroll can still be on an accelerated schedule.

What are the two thresholds?

$25,000.00 and $100,000.00. Below the first is a regular remitter, between them is threshold 1, and at or above the second is threshold 2.

When does a threshold 1 remitter pay?

Twice a month: the 25th for pay dates in the 1st to the 15th, and the 10th of the following month for the rest.

When does a threshold 2 remitter pay?

Four times a month, on the third working day after the 7th, the 14th, the 21st and the last day of the month.

Can a small employer remit quarterly?

Where the figure is under $3,000.00 and the compliance record over the preceding twelve months is perfect, the Agency can assign a quarterly schedule. It is assigned rather than elected.

What if the due date is a weekend or a holiday?

The remittance is on time if it reaches the Agency on the next business day.

What if no wages were paid in the period?

The period is still part of the account. Reporting it at nil is what keeps a non-filing notice and an estimate from following.

Is payroll part of the nil T2 fee?

No. The fee covers the corporate income tax return. Payroll is a separate programme account with its own filings.

title: Shareholder Loan Income Inclusion Calculator | 15(2)
content:
Shareholders

Shareholder Loan Income Inclusion Calculator

Miss the one-year deadline and the whole loan is income, in the shareholder hands and in the year the money was taken.

One year after the year endThe shareholder’s incomeA 20(1)(j) deduction on repaymentThe corporate year can be nil

Written and reviewed by Sharad Gondaliya, CPA (Ontario), CPA Ontario Membership 61040184.

Start Nil T2 Filing NOW

Last reviewed: November 23, 2026

The loan

Enter the year end and the amount, and answer both questions.

Gondaliya CPA Professional Corporation is a registered EFILE electronic filer. Returns are prepared and transmitted in Canada. Credentials are never shared and never used offshore.

The Window Hangs Off the Year End, Which Is Why It Varies

Subsection 15(2) includes the amount of a loan from a corporation to a shareholder in income. Subsection 15(2.6) takes it back out where the loan is repaid within one year after the end of the corporation’s taxation year in which the loan was made. The deadline therefore hangs off the year end rather than off the date of the loan, which is what makes the available time vary so widely.

A loan taken the day after a December 31 year end has almost two years to run. A loan taken on December 30 has one year and a day. Same provision, same corporation, and the second one is the shape that goes wrong.

Corporation’s year endLoan madeRepay byTime available
December 31, 2025January 2, 2026December 31, 2026Almost two years
December 31, 2025December 30, 2026December 31, 2026One day
June 30, 2026July 1, 2026June 30, 2027Almost two years
June 30, 2026June 29, 2026June 30, 2027One year and a day
February 28, 2026March 1, 2026February 28, 2027Almost two years

The shareholder loan repayment deadline calculator computes that date on its own, and the shareholder loan balance checker and the due to versus due from shareholder checker cover the balance and which side of the balance sheet it sits on.

The Amount Lands on a Personal Return, in an Earlier Year

Two things about the inclusion are easy to get backwards, and getting either backwards changes the advice entirely.

The first is whose income it is. The amount is included in the shareholder’s income under subsection 15(2). It is not corporate income and it does not appear on the T2. A corporation that earned nothing, claimed nothing and lent its shareholder money that was never repaid still has a nil tax year, and the problem sits entirely on the personal side.

The second is which year. The inclusion is for the year the loan was received, not the year the deadline passed. That is very often a personal return filed and assessed long ago, which is why the practical consequence is a reassessment of an earlier year rather than a line on the next one. A later repayment does not undo it: paragraph 20(1)(j) gives a deduction in the year of repayment, which only helps if there is income in that year to apply it against.

The amount goes in the shareholder’s income for the year the loan was received, which is why the consequence usually lands on a personal return that was filed long ago.

The Exceptions, and the Benefit That Survives Them

Three routes keep an amount out of subsection 15(2). Repayment inside the 15(2.6) window is the common one, provided the repayment is not part of a series of loans and repayments, because paying a balance down at a year end and drawing it again afterwards does not satisfy the subsection. Subsection 15(2.3) covers a loan made in the ordinary course of a lending business. Subsection 15(2.4) covers certain loans to an employee, including one to acquire a dwelling or shares of the employer, where bona fide repayment arrangements were made when the loan was granted.

A separate charge survives all three. Where a loan carries no interest, or interest below the prescribed rate, subsection 80.4(2) brings an interest benefit into income for the period the loan is outstanding. The prescribed rate is set quarterly, so the amount is not computed on this page; the point is that repaying inside the deadline answers subsection 15(2) and does not answer subsection 80.4(2).

On the corporate side the balance is a reportable transaction with a shareholder, which the Schedule 11 shareholder transactions checker covers, and the shareholder may need naming on Schedule 50, which the Schedule 50 shareholder threshold checker settles. Nil T2 filing at $300.00 plus applicable sales tax per tax year covers the corporate return for the year including those schedules where they are required, and the guide to Schedule 50 and shareholder reporting covers the disclosure side.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much of a shareholder loan is included in income?

The whole amount of the loan or indebtedness, where no exception applies and it is not repaid within the subsection 15(2.6) window.

Whose income is it included in?

The shareholder’s. It is not corporate income and it does not appear on the T2.

Which tax year does it land in?

The year the loan was received, not the year the repayment deadline passed. That often means an earlier personal return being reassessed.

What is the repayment deadline?

One year after the end of the corporation’s taxation year in which the loan was made.

Does repaying it later fix the inclusion?

It does not reverse the inclusion. Paragraph 20(1)(j) gives a deduction in the year of repayment instead.

Can the corporation still file a nil return?

Yes. A corporation that earned nothing and claimed nothing has a nil tax year whatever happened to the loan on the shareholder’s side.

What if the loan is repaid and drawn again?

A repayment that is part of a series of loans and repayments does not satisfy subsection 15(2.6), so the amount stays within subsection 15(2).

Are there exceptions to the inclusion?

Yes. Subsection 15(2.3) for a loan made in the ordinary course of a lending business, and subsection 15(2.4) for certain employee loans with bona fide repayment arrangements.

Is there interest on top of the inclusion?

A separate benefit can arise under subsection 80.4(2) where the loan carries no interest or interest below the prescribed rate. The rate is set quarterly and is not computed here.

Does the loan have to be reported on the T2?

The balance is a transaction with a shareholder and is reportable on the corporate return, which is a different thing from being corporate income.
